The gating strategies of our FCM have been shown in Supplementary Figs. 18 and 19. The antibodies have been summarized in Supplementary Data 11.

Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence
Tissue chip of paired melanoma and paracancerous tissues was purchased from WEIAOBIO (Catalog: ZL-MEL963). All uses of human material have been approved. The IRB approval (approval number: LLS M-15-01) has been provided by the ethics committee of Shanghai Zhuoli Biotechnology Co., Ltd, whose general distributor is the WEIAOBIO. Tumor tissues from humanely euthanized mice were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 3µm, hydrated, and underwent antigen retrieval.

For immunohistochemistry, the sections were pre-treated with 3% H2O2 to remove endogenous peroxidase activity. Then the cell slides were blocked with goat serum and incubated with desired antibody and detect antibody successively. The cell slides were incubated with DAB substrate, counterstained by hematoxylin, dehydrated, and mounted. The following antibodies were used: TMEM175 antibody (Proteintech, 19925-1-AP), cleaved caspase-3 (Asp175) antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 9661L), caspase-1 p10 antibody (SANTA CRUZ, sc-56036), IL-1β (3A6) Mouse antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 12242S), HRP anti-rabbit IgG antibody (ServiceBio, GB23303), and HRP anti-mouse IgG antibody (ServiceBio, G1214). For immunofluorescence, the slides were incubated with NK1.1 mouse mAb (Thermo Fisher, 14-5941-82) and CD8 rat mAb (Abcam, ab25478) overnight. Then the slides were incubated with AF488 anti-rat IgG (Thermo Fisher, A-11006) and Cy3 anti-mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher, M30010). Finally, the slides were incubated with DAPI (Beyotime, C1005) and mounted. The TMEM175 positive area, caspase-1 p10 positive area, IL-1β positive area, cleaved caspase-3 positive area, CD8-AF488 positive area, and NK1.1-Cy3 positive area were measured by ImageJ software. The antibodies have been summarized in Supplementary Data 11.

Cross-presentation assay
B16-F10-OVA cells were implanted in wild type C57BL/6J mice and grew for 10 days to prime CD8+ T cells. Then the mice were humanely euthanized to collect the spleens, from which the lymphocytes were separated by Mouse lymphocyte separation medium (DAKEWE, DKW33-R0100). The lymphocytes (1×106) were labeled by CFSE kit (Thermo Fisher) and then cultured with BMDMs (1×106) with IL-2 (20U/mL) (Novoprotein, CK24) and B16-F10-OVA cell debris (2.5×105/mL) for 48h with or without IL-1β (500pg/mL) and IL-18 (500pg/mL). After 48h, the cells were harvested and stained by H-2Kb OVA Tetramer (MBL, TS-5001-1C), antibodies, and LIVE/DEAD Fixable Near-IR Dead Cell Stain Kit (Thermo Fisher, L34975). The cells were analyzed by ACEA NovoCyte (ACEA Biosciences). The culture medium was collected for ELISA assay.

For the siRNA silencing, in vitro cultured WT or Tmem175−/− BMDMs were transfected with siRNA (GenePharma) targeting Myd88 (sense: 5′-GAAGCGACUGAUUCCUAUUTT-3′ anti-sense: 5′-AAUAG GAAUCAGUCGCUUCTT-3′) or Csf2rb (sense: 5′-GCCUGCAUUGG GAAACUCATT-3′ anti-sense: 5′-UGAGUUUCCCAAUGCAGGCTT-3′) via Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher, 13778030). The oligonucleotide sequences have been summarized in Supplementary Data 11.

In vitro stimulation of inflammasomes
B16-F10 tumor cell debris was the main inflammasome stimulator in our experiment. The concentration of cell debris was 2.5×105/mL. The harvested cells were repeatedly blown by syringes followed by two freeze-thaw cycles to generate cell debris. BMDMs (1×106) were activated by 500ng/mL LPS (Sigma, L2880) for 4h, then the medium was discarded, and the BMDMs were treated with cell debris for a desired period of time. During the treatment of cell debris, VX-765, CA-074, or KCl were added, whose final concentrations were 10µg/mL, 100µM, and 40mM respectively. For positive control, 10µM Nigericin (MCE, HY-127019) was added after LPS stimulation. For calcium chelation, cells were incubated with 20µM BAPTA-AM (MCE, HY-100545) for 30min after the LPS treatment. For ROS inhibition, cells were incubated with 10mM NAC (MCE, HY-B0215) during the cell debris treatment. For Bafilomycin A1 treatment, cells were incubated with 1µM Bafilomycin A1 (MCE, HY-100558) during the cell debris treatment. For the treatment of chitosan, BMDMs or peritoneal macrophages were activated by 500ng/mL LPS (Sigma, L2880) for 4h and then treated with 40µg/mL chitosan (Sigma, 448869) for 5h. For the treatment of aluminium hydroxide (Invivogen, vac-alu-50), BMDMs were activated by 500ng/mL LPS (Sigma, L2880) for 4h and then treated with 300µg/mL aluminium hydroxide for a desired period of time. For the treatment of B16-F10 supernatant, BMDMs were activated by 500ng/mL LPS (Sigma, L2880) for 4h and then treated with 25% volume of filtered B16-F10 supernatant overnight.

ELISA
Cell culture supernatants were analyzed by Mouse IL-1beta Uncoated ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, 88-7013A-88), Mouse TNF Uncoated ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, 88-7324-88), and Mouse IFN gamma “Femto-HS” High Sensitivity Uncoated ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, 88-8314-88) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Western blot
For the western blot analysis of cell lysis, BMDMs were lysed by RIPA (Beyotime, P0013B) and boiled with 1× SDS buffer (Beyotime, P0015L) for 5min at 95°C. Protein lysates were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore, IPVH00010). The membranes were probed by desired antibodies.

For the western blot analysis of cell supernatant, total proteins in the cell supernatant were precipitated by an equal volume of 10% trichloroacetic acid (TCA). The protein precipitants were washed by cold acetone three times. Then precipitants were subjected to air-drying for 5min. The precipitants were dissolved by alkaline 1 × SDS buffer (Beyotime, P0015L) plus 200mM DTT (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R0861) and then boiled for 5min at 95°C. The grayscale values of TMEM175, β-actin, caspase-1 p10, IL-18 p24, ASC polymer, and cathepsin B were measured by ImageJ software. If the immunoblotting included β-actin, the results were presented as the ratio of the target protein/β-actin; otherwise, the grayscale values of the target protein were presented directly.

The following antibodies were used: TMEM175 mouse mAb (Proteintech, 68172-1-Ig), caspase-1 rabbit mAb (Abcam, 3345-1), IL-18 mouse mAb (LSBio, LS-C179849), β-actin mouse mAb (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-47778), anti-rabbit IgG (HRP) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31460), anti-mouse IgG (HRP) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31430), and anti-rabbit IgG-Fc (HRP) (SinoBiological, SSA003). The antibodies have been summarized in Supplementary Data 11.

Co-immunoprecipitation
After the desired treatment, BMDMs were lysed by RIPA. Protein lysates were incubated with 1µg/mL rabbit IgG isotype (Cell Signaling Technology, 3900S) and 20µL Protein A+G Agarose (Beyotime, P2012) at 4°C for 30min to avoid non-specific combination. The lysates were centrifuged to remove the agarose beads and incubated with 1µg/mL NLRP3 rabbit mAb (Cell Signaling Technology, 15101S) at 4°C overnight, during which 5mM EDTA-Na2 was added to the desired group. For negative control, the lysates were incubated overnight with 1µg/mL isotype rabbit IgG. Afterward, the lysates were incubated with 20µL Protein A+G Agarose (Beyotime, P2012) at 4°C for 3h. The beads were washed 3 times with RIPA. Finally, the beads were resuspended in 1× SDS buffer and boiled for 5min at 95°C.

The following antibodies were used: Cathepsin B rabbit mAb (Cell Signaling Technology, 31718S), ASC mouse mAb (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-514414), NLRP3 rabbit mAb (Cell Signaling Technology, 15101S), Rabbit IgG isotype (Cell Signaling Technology, 3900S), anti-rabbit IgG (HRP) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31460), anti-mouse IgG (HRP) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31430), and anti-rabbit IgG-Fc (HRP) (SinoBiological, SSA003). The antibodies have been summarized in Supplementary Data 11.

Transcriptome analysis
Tmem175−/− and WT BMDMs were cultured, harvested, and lysed in TRIzol (Invitrogen, 15596018CN). Novogene Bioinformatics Institute, Beijing, China, performed the RNA extraction and sequencing. The raw data were processed by adapter trimming, and reads were filtered by trimgalore version 0.5.0 to ensure data quality. The reads were mapped to Mus_musculus.GRCm38.dna.toplevel.fa and annotated with Mus_musculus.GRCm38.98.gtf.

To identify differentially expressed genes between Tmem175−/− and WT groups, fold change (FC) was calculated. The cut-off number of log2FC was set to be 1. The P values were calculated by likelihood ratio test, and adjusted by Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The differentially expressed genes were further annotated using Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes database. The P values of GO and KEGG analysis were calculated by Fisher’s exact test and adjusted by Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.

The RNA-seq of the co-culture system was performed by DNBSEQ-T7 (MGITech). Clean reads were obtained by removing the adaptor sequences, reads with >5% ambiguous bases, and low-quality reads containing more than 20% of bases with qualities of <13. The clean reads were aligned to mouse genome (version: GRCh38 NCBI) using hisat2. The DESeq algorithm was used to filter the differentially expressed genes (FoldChange >1.1 or <0.9, FDR <0.05). The P values were calculated by Negative binomial distribution test, and adjusted by Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. For GO enrichment analysis, GO annotations were downloaded from NCBI, UniProt, and the Gene Ontology. Significant GO categories were identified by Fisher’s exact test, and the p-value was corrected by FDR through Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Significant KEGG pathways were selected by Fisher’s exact test, and the significance thresholds were defined by p-value and FDR through Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.

Electron microscopy
BMDMs were harvested, fixed with 3% glutaraldehyde, and re-fixed with 1% osmium tetroxide. The pellets were dehydrated with a series of acetone and embedded in Ep812. The ultrathin sections were cut by a diamond knife and stained by uranyl acetate and lead citrate. Images were taken by JEM-1400-FLASH Transmission Electron Microscope.

Lysosomal pH determination
The determination of lysosomal pH was performed using LysoSensor Yellow/Blue DND-160 (Invitrogen, L7545) according to manufacturers’ instructions. BMDMs were seeded in non-transparent 96-well plates. BMDMs were incubated with 5µM LysoSensor Yellow/Blue DND-160 for 5min after cell debris stimulation. Then the cells were washed twice by phenol red-free 1640 (Gibco, 11835030). The plates were read by Microplate Reader (PerkinElmer). Two fluorescence intensities, 329nm excitation/440nm emission and 384nm excitation/540nm emission, were collected. The ratio of 440nm/540nm was calculated for every well. We created a standard curve for pH calculation with a series of solutions with known pH at 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. The LysoSensor Yellow/Blue DND-160 fluorescents were collected, and the 440nm/540nm ratio of each solution was calculated and used to create the standard curve. The values of lysosomal pH were calculated by referring to the standard curve.

Lysosomal calcium determination
The determination of lysosomal calcium determination was performed using AF488-dextran (Invitrogen, D34682) and rhod-dextran (AAT Bioquest, 20451) according to previous report86. Briefly, BMDMs were seeded in non-transparent 96-well plates and incubated with 0.1mg/mL rhod-dextran and 0.2mg/mL AF488-dextran overnight. The cells were then washed twice and stimulated with LPS and B16-F10 tumor cell debris as mentioned above in phenol red-free 1640 (Gibco, 11835030). The plates were read by a Microplate Reader (PerkinElmer). At the same time, standard wells with known calcium concentration were used as control. Two fluorescence intensities, 543nm excitation/560nm emission and 488nm excitation/530nm emission, were collected. The lysosomal calcium concentrations were calculated using the following equations: [Ca2+] = Kd × (R - Rmin) / (Rmax - R) × (Sf2 / Sb2). R was the ratio of 560nm/530nm for a single well at a certain time point; Rmin was the lowest 560nm/530nm ratio; Rmax was the highest 560nm/530nm ratio of a saturating calcium concentration. Sf2 and Sb2 showed fluorescence of 530nm in the absence and presence of calcium, respectively. Kd is the dissociation constant determined by the standard curve with pH at 5, which equals to the concentration of calcium at which 560nm fluorescence of rhod-dextran reached 50% brightness. In the desired wells, 1µM Bafilomycin A1 (MCE, HY-100558) was added during the cell debris treatment.

Cytoplasmic calcium determination
The determination of cytoplasmic calcium was performed using Fluo-4-AM (Invitrogen, F14201). Briefly, BMDMs were seeded in non-transparent 96-well plates. BMDMs were incubated with 2µM Fluo-4-AM for 30min after cell debris stimulation. Then the cells were washed twice in phenol red-free 1640 (Gibco, 11835030). The plates were read by a Microplate Reader (PerkinElmer). Fluorescence intensity 480nm excitation/525nm emission was collected. The fluorescence of Fluo-4 was positively related to the concentration of cytoplasmic calcium; thus, the final results were presented as the ratio of 525nm fluorescence in each group to the average 525nm fluorescence in the blank group. In the desired wells, 1µM Bafilomycin A1 (MCE, HY-100558) or 100µM CA-074 (MCE, HY-103350) was added during the cell debris treatment.

Confocal microscope
BMDMs were seeded in glass slips and treated by LPS and B16-F10 tumor cell debris mentioned above. The cells were fixed and permeabilized by Cytofix/Cytoperm Fixation/Permeabilization Kit (BD bioscience, 554714). Then the cells were incubated with the desired antibodies overnight and the desired fluorescent secondary antibodies at room temperature. For cathepsin B rabbit mAb (Cell Signaling Technology, 31718S), the fluorescent secondary antibodies were Cy3 goat anti-rabbit IgG (Abcam, ab98416). For cathepsin D mAb (HUABIO, ET1608-49) and cathepsin L mAb (HUABIO, HA722063), the fluorescent secondary antibodies were AF488 goat anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-11034). Nuclei were stained with DAPI (Beyotime, C1005). Imaging was performed using laser scanning confocal microscope (Olympus), and the images were analyzed using CellSens Dimension Software (Olympus).

ROS detection
The determination of ROS was performed using ROS probe, H2DCFDA (Invitrogen, D399). Briefly, BMDMs were seeded in non-transparent 96-well plates. BMDMs were incubated with 1µM H2DCFDA for 30min after cell debris stimulation. Then the cells were washed twice in phenol red-free 1640 (Gibco, 11835030). The plates were read by a Microplate Reader (PerkinElmer). Fluorescence intensity 488nm excitation/520nm emission was collected. The fluorescence intensity was positively related to the concentration of ROS.

Molecular dynamics simulation
The model of PYD domain from ASC was downloaded from protein data bank (PDB: 2N1F). The model of PYD domain from NLRP3 was built by Swiss-model87. The GMQE was 0.88, and the QMEANS was 0.81±0.05, indicating a reliable structure generation. The molecular docking was performed using HDock88, in which the docking score was 176.33 kcal/mol. The molecular docking result was used as the initiating conformation in the molecular dynamics simulation.

Gromacs 2019.689 was applied, and Amber14SB was selected as protein force field. The water model was established by TIP3P. Ten calcium ions were randomly added, and the sodium ion/chloride system was founded. The particle-mesh Ewald algorithm was used for electrostatic calculations, in which the system was minimized via steepest descent algorithm for 50,000 steps. The cut-off distance of both Coulomb force and the van der Waals radii was 1.4nm. Canonical ensemble (NVT) and constant-temperature, constant-pressure ensemble (NPT) were adopted. Molecular dynamics simulation was performed for 100ns at normal temperature and pressure. The results were displayed by PyMOL 2.5.190 and LigPlot 2.191.

Statistical analysis
Results from two or three independent experiments are presented as average values ± SEM. The number of biological replicates is shown in the figure legends. All statistical analyses were performed by linear regression, two-sided unpaired t-test (for 2 groups), one-way ANOVA (for 3 groups), or two-way ANOVA (for ≥2 variables or ≥4 groups) using GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Prism Software Inc., La Jolla). The statistical methods to calculate the statistical significances were indicated in the figure legends.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this MS by Zhang et al., the authors investigated the roles of lysosomal TMEM175 channels in tumor growth through an interactive regulation of tumor microenvironment. Conditional knockout of Tmem175 in mouse macrophages resulted in reduced tumor weight and metastasis. This effect was reversed by VX-765, a broad-spectrum inflammasome inhibitor, suggesting that inflammasome signaling is essential for the anti-tumor effects mediated by TMEM175 deficiency. It was claimed that in Tmem175 KO cells, lysosomes were hypo-acidified, resulting in increased lysosomal cathepsin B (CTSB) leakage and Ca2+ efflux. The subsequent cytosolic Ca2+ elevation was proposed to regulate cell debris-activated inflammation, as both CTSB inhibitors and membrane-permeable Ca2+ chelator BAPTA-AM completely eliminated the differences between WT and KO cells. Overall, there were some interesting observations in the study, but many experimental details and controls were missing. Hence, the evidence presented in this article is insufficient to support the conclusions drawn in many sections.
Major Concerns:
1. In Figure 1, the weak band intensity observed in the western blot for the Tmem175-/- group was attributed to the presence of remaining exons 1-4. However, one would expect a size-shifted band in KO samples. It was not clear whether the antibody used was specific, as KO efficiency appeared to be only slightly more than 50%, judging from the biochemical validation.
2. In Figures 6 and 7, both CA-074 and BAPTA-AM abolished the differences in cell debris-activated inflammation between WT and KO cells. What is the relationship between cytosolic CTSB accumulation and Ca2+ elevation? Additional controls are necessary to delineate the relationship between these two events. For instance, what is the effect on CTSB activity following BAPTA-AM treatment, and what is the effect of CA-074 treatment on cytosolic Ca2+ elevation?
3. In Figure 7, it was suggested that elevated lysosomal pH is associated with the efflux of lysosomal Ca2+. Can pre-treatment with Baf-A1, a V-ATPase inhibitor, mimic all the effects of TMEM175 KO?
4. As mentioned in Discussion, the effect of TMEM175 KO on lysosomal pH is controversial. What is the basal lysosomal pH of BMDMs without LPS treatment? It was also not clear about the effects of LPS and cell debris treatments on lysosomal pH and Ca2+ in WT and KO cells.
5. In Figures 7b and 7c, the authors showed decreases in lysosomal pH and calcium concentrations. However, most Ca2+ dyes are known to be pH-sensitive. How can you separate the effects of your treatment on Ca2+ versus pH?
6. For the electrophysiological recordings in Figure 1, it was difficult to evaluate the results without providing detailed recording solutions and protocols. How did you know whether the currents were not caused by leakage?
7. In Figure 6g, there was no significant difference for the leakage of cathepsin B between WT and Tmem175 KO groups. Statistical analysis was missing. What was the rationale that only CTSB, but not other cathepsins, e.g., CTSD or CTSL, was investigated? Previous studies suggested that CTSL might be more relevant for lysosome membrane permeability.
8. The levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were high in Tmem175-/- BMDMs. Do ROS contribute to the observed phenotypes?
Minor Concerns:
1. What does the time point "0" represent in Figure 7a? The Y-axis indicates lysosomal pH, but it is unclear on how lysosomal pH was calibrated in the study.
2. In Figure 9, are you sure about the direction of K+ flow across lysosomal membranes? Cytosolic K+ concentration is known to be as high as 150 mM.
3. In Figure 1e, why did the scale of the ratio start from 0.2?
4. There was lack of statistical analysis in Figure 7c.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this study by Zhang et al., the authors elucidate a critical role for TMEM175 within myeloid cells in orchestrating the anti-tumour immune response. The myeloid-specific Tmem175 knockout in murine models exhibited notable anti-tumour efficacy, accompanied by a reconfiguration of the tumour microenvironment. Furthermore, TMEM175 ablation impaired lysosomal acidification and potentiated cross-presentation of tumour antigens. These findings, highlighting the therapeutic promise of targeting TMEM175 in myeloid cells, are both innovative and promising. Nevertheless, the manuscript would benefit from refined data presentation and an augmented mechanistic investigation, as outlined below.
Major Concerns:
Clinical Relevance: The study proposes TMEM175 as an intriguing target for tumour immunotherapy. However, it remains unclear whether TMEM175 is differentially expressed between normal and cancerous tissues. Additionally, does TMEM175 deficiency influence the polarisation of tissue-resident macrophages?
In Figures 2 and 3, TMEM175 deficiency demonstrates anti-tumour effects by impeding tumour growth and metastasis, with concurrent alterations in tumour-associated macrophage (TAM) composition and T-cell infiltration. These findings, however, are predominantly observational. A mechanistic elucidation is necessary to substantiate whether, and through what pathways, TMEM175 deficiency attenuates the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Does TMEM175 directly modulate TAM polarisation? What are the underlying molecular mechanisms? Moreover, the functional contributions of distinct immune cell populations to the observed anti-tumour effects remain ambiguous. Depletion of TAMs and T-cells would substantiate these findings.
An enigmatic observation lies in the insensitivity of B16-F10 tumours to inflammasome inhibition (via VX-765) juxtaposed with their heightened sensitivity to inflammasome stimulation (through chitosan), as illustrated in Figure 4.
The antigen cross-presentation data presented in Figure 5 are perplexing. Tmem175-/- bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) markedly induce proliferation of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells, even in the absence of B16-F10 OVA cell debris. The addition of B16-F10 OVA debris results in only a minimal further increase in T cell proliferation. This suggests that the observed T cell proliferation and activation may occur via mechanisms beyond antigen cross-presentation.
Minor Points:
1. In Figure 1d, there remains a residual band, albeit weaker than wild-type, in BMDMs from Tmem175-/- mice. The authors attribute this to residual expression from exons 1-4; however, the band appears at the same molecular weight as full-length TMEM175. Additional validation is warranted to confirm effective knockout of Tmem175 in myeloid cells.
2. Vehicle controls are conspicuously absent in Figure 4j.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overall comments:
In this manuscript, Zhang, et al investigate the role of TMEM175 in macrophages and tumors reporting macrophage-specific TMEM175 deficiency inhibited tumor growth through promoting M1-like polarization and the recruitment of T cells and NKs. In addition, they found TMEM175 KO BMDMs showed enhanced tumor antigen cross-presentation. To further explore the mechanism, authors determined the importance of inflammasome activation in macrophages and found TMEM175 deficiency inhibited lysosomal acidification and promoted lysosomal calcium efflux, leading to increased ASC-NLRP3 interaction. As a possible therapeutic strategy, macrophage-specific TMEM175 KO mice had better therapeutic response to anti-PDL1 therapy.
Their work is interesting and provides new insights into the function of macrophage TMEM175 in regulation of the tumor microenvironment. Their finding that macrophage-specific KO reduced tumor growth and improved the therapeutic effect of anti-PDL1 enhance the translational potential of their study. However, the mechanism by which TMEM175 promotes the anti-tumor immunity is too diffuse and complicated and not well-supported at several places. The mechanistic aspect can be strengthened with some additional experiments and significant reorganizations as I detail below:
Major points:
The authors made a significant effort in exploring the mechanisms by which TMEM175 deficiency promotes the anti-tumor immunity. However, their concept includes multiple parallel pathways (inflammasome activation by cathepsin, ROS, and calcium efflux; cross-presentation of tumor antigens; and autophagy dysfunction) which leads to an unfocused assessment resulting in confusion of the reader. In addition, beyond usage of VX-765 to test the importance of inflammasome activation during tumor progression, other pathways are not fully characterized in their tumor models. It’s not clear how much each pathway contributes to the anti-tumor immunity in TMEM175 KO macrophages, or this effect is just a simple mixture of phenotypes from different pathways.
1) The authors indicate that increased IL-1β and IL-18 secreted from TMEM175 KO macrophages drive the recruitment and activation of T cells and NK cells in TME. To support their conclusion, the anti-tumor immunity in vivo should be evaluated using neutralizing antibodies or ways to perturb this cytokine signaling.
2) The authors raise three hypotheses about how TMEM175 deficiency leads to increased inflammasome activation: increased cathepsin B leakage, higher ROS levels, and elevated cytosolic calcium. Although all three mechanisms may result from TMEM175-induced lysosomal dysfunction, the effects of inhibitors (CA-074, BAPTA-AM, etc) for these pathways on blocking inflammasome activation should be evaluated to identify whether there’s a dominant pathway responsible for the pro-inflammatory phenotype in TMEM175 KO macrophages. Moreover, the dominant inhibitor should be tested in vivo for the effect of pathways on anti-tumor immunity and tumor growth. VX-765 is only a general inhibitor of caspase-1. For the precise machinery of anti-tumor immunity, siRNA-mediated gene silencing in macrophages should be conducted to verify the pharmacological inhibition data, and the anti-tumor effect of macrophage conditional depletion of the predominant pathway should be evaluated in vivo. In this way, the manuscript becomes more focused on a predominant pathways as the key mechanism underlying their phenotype. By evaluating all types of pathways in superficial ways, it leaves more to be desired and confuses the reader.
3) Authors also demonstrated TMEM175 deficiency augmented the cross-presentation of tumor antigens. The in vitro work is nice but without evaluation of the effect of this pathway on anti-tumor immunity and tumor growth weakens their conclusion. In addition, authors mentioned the elevated cross-presentation signal in TMEM175 KO macrophages can be enhanced by IL-1β and IL-18 but didn’t provide any explanation. Does it mean those cytokines promote phagocytosis, or the antigen-presentation relies on inflammasome activation? The utilization of siRNA may help answer these questions.
4) The data about autophagy dysfunction and inflammasome activation is very superficial and lacks the evaluation of IL-1β secretion, so can be removed from the revised manuscript and only mentioned in the discussion. Again, by doing superficial work on multiple pathways as a mechanism is not focused.
5) The study on PYD-PYD interaction (Fig. 7f-k) seems redundant and not directly linked to their main findings.
Minor points:
1) Similarly, the Discussion Section is too long and includes lots of review about TMEM175 and lysosomal dysfunction. Based on their findings, authors should focus on how TMEM175 expression is regulated in macrophages during tumor progression and what area therapeutic strategies can be developed.
2) The description of generating conditional TMEM175 mice can be moved to the Method Section or Supplemental figure legends and not main figures.

This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

6. For the electrophysiological recordings in Figure 1, it was difficult to evaluate
the results without providing detailed recording solutions and protocols. How did
you know whether the currents were not caused by leakage?
Response: Thank you for your question. We provided additional details for our whole-
organelle voltage-clamp recording in our method section. The lysosomal
electrophysiological recordings were performed referring to the protocol published by
Cheng-Chang Chen et al. (Patch-clamp technique to characterize ion channels in
enlarged individual endolysosomes, PMID: 28726848). In commonly studied whole-
cell electrophysiology, the leakage currents are usually caused by incomplete gigaseal
formation or loss of seal during the whole-cell mode. For incomplete gigaseal formation,
it was very easy to form complete gigaseal (resistance around 8-20 GΩ) by the fire-
polished glass pipettes in our whole-lysosomal mode. For loss of seal, the situation
seems to be different between whole-cell and whole-lysosomal electrophysiology. In
whole-cell electrophysiology, the pipette tips could be partially separated from the cell
membrane to cause leakage current and the incomplete seal could be maintained for a
period of time, but we did not observe such situation in our whole-lysosomal
electrophysiology. When the pipette tips were separated from the lysosomal membranes
through slightly positive pressure or moving the pipette tips, the current dramatically
increased and the lysosomes sometimes ruptured. We speculate that lysosomal
membranes are more fragile than cell membrane, therefore incomplete seal could not
exist stably either during the gigaseal formation nor during the whole-lysosomal mode.
Thus our results were not likely to be the leakage currents.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: In this revised manuscript, the authors have performed several new experiments to address the reviewers' concerns, and the revised manuscript is improved. The roles of TMEM175 in anti-tumor immunity via inflammasome activation are convincingly established. However, the proposed mechanisms that link the channel properties of lysosomal TMEM175 with Ca²⁺ dys-homeostasis and oxidative stress are still not clear. In the new working model in Figure 10, the authors now claim that there is no lysosomal K⁺ defect associated with TMEM175 deficiency. Instead, they attribute the abnormalities in Ca²⁺ and ROS levels to a lysosomal pH defect (hypo-acidification). It should be noted that the basal lysosomal pH was reported to be normal in early TMEM175 studies (PMID 26317472) but decreased (hyper-acidification) in more recent studies (e.g., PMID: 35750034, 35333573). However, the new data in the revision showed that the basal lysosomal pH was elevated (see Figure 8), which contradicts all previous studies. Additionally, lysosomal pH in macrophages was reported to be more acidic upon M-CSF treatment (PMID: 17314396). These discrepancies must be addressed if the authors aim to provide mechanistic explanations for the role of a lysosomal K⁺/H⁺ channel in anti-tumor immunity. It is also important to note that Ca²⁺ defects were proposed to cause ROS elevation, which in turn promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 secretion. Yet, lysosomal Ca²⁺ levels were shown to be normal in TMEM175 knockout (KO) cells (Figure 8b). These findings suggest that the Ca²⁺/ROS/inflammasome effects may be secondary to lysosomal dysfunction associated with TMEM175 deficiency. Additionally, TMEM175 overexpression was reported to cause lysosomal hypo-acidification (e.g., PMID: 35750034, 35333573). This raises the question: would TMEM175 overexpression also exert effects in anti-tumor immunity? Some of the specific comments were not satisfactorily addressed. For instance, in the response to major concern 1, this reviewer was unable to find the mentioned 40-55 kD band in the attached Figure 1. Regarding the response to major concern 6, membrane leak can be easily investigated using Na⁺ or NMDG⁺ containing recording solutions, as neither of these ions is permeable to TMEM175 (PMID 26317472).Overall, while the revised manuscript addresses some of the reviewers' concerns, several critical issues regarding the mechanisms linking TMEM175 to Ca²⁺ dys-homeostasis, oxidative stress, and lysosomal pH remain unresolved and require further clarification.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have done an excellent job revising the manuscript, and my previous comments have been adequately addressed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overall comments:
The authors have addressed my comments including adding more data and discussion to improve the manuscript. However, a few issues remain to address in the revision. These are listed below:
1) Authors did a great job to evaluate the effect of CA-074 and BAPTA-AM on the inhibition of anti-tumor immunity in Tmem175-/- mice. However, without an in vivo experiment using NAC, the contribution of ROS to the anti-tumor immunity is still unclear.
2) Authors did a great amount of work on the mechanism by which cross-presentation signals in TMEM175 KO macrophages was enhanced by IL-1β and IL-18. However, the explanation is still unclear and too complicated. If authors thought NF-kappaB pathway is the main mediator of IL-1β/IL18-enhanced cross-presentation signal in macrophages, a treatment of Myd88 siRNA or related inhibitors will help determine their hypothesis. Similarly, the roles of DEGs they found could also be verified in macrophages with siRNA.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear editor,
Thank you for your letter and the reviewers comments concerning our manuscript
Deficiency of lysosomal TMEM175 in myeloid macrophages exerts anti-tumor
immunity via inflammasome and cross-presentation pathway (NCOMMS-24-59454B)
submitted to Nature communications. The comments are very helpful for us to
improve our manuscript. Newly revised portions are highlighted in yellow. The point-
by-point response for the reviewers’ comments are listed as follows.
Reviewer #1
1. In this revised manuscript, the authors have performed several new experiments
to address the reviewers' concerns, and the revised manuscript is improved. The
roles of TMEM175 in anti-tumor immunity via inflammasome activation are
convincingly established. However, the proposed mechanisms that link the channel
properties of lysosomal TMEM175 with Ca²⁺ dys-homeostasis and oxidative stress
are still not clear. In the new working model in Figure 10, the authors now claim
that there is no lysosomal K⁺ defect associated with TMEM175 deficiency. Instead,
they attribute the abnormalities in Ca²⁺ and ROS levels to a lysosomal pH defect
(hypo-acidification). It should be noted that the basal lysosomal pH was reported
to be normal in early TMEM175 studies (PMID 26317472) but decreased (hyper-
acidification) in more recent studies (e.g., PMID: 35750034, 35333573). However,
the new data in the revision showed that the basal lysosomal pH was elevated (see
Figure 8), which contradicts all previous studies. Additionally, lysosomal pH in
macrophages was reported to be more acidic upon M-CSF treatment (PMID:
17314396). These discrepancies must be addressed if the authors aim to provide
mechanistic explanations for the role of a lysosomal K⁺/H⁺ channel in anti-tumor
immunity.
Response: Thank you for your kind and constructive comments. We appreciate your
professional insights into the current literature on TMEM175. In our response, we first
address the seemingly contradictory findings reported in previous studies and then
explain our results. To address your comments thoroughly, we have repeated the
relevant experiments using improved methodologies and have updated the manuscript
with additional discussion.
In the earlier articles (TMEM175 Is an Organelle K(+) Channel Regulating
Lysosomal Function. Chunlei Cang et al. Cell. 2015, PMID: 26317472 and
TMEM175 deficiency impairs lysosomal and mitochondrial function and increases
α-synuclein aggregation. Sarah Jinn et al. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2017, PMID:
28193887), lysosomal acidification was reported to be impaired in TMEM175
knockout cells under starvation conditions. However, under nutrient-rich (fed)
conditions, lysosomal pH was found to be slightly lower in TMEM175 KO cells
compared to wild-type (WT) cells. Additionally, in another article (A growth-factor-
activated lysosomal K+ channel regulates Parkinson's pathology. Jinhong Wie et al.
Nature. 2021 PMID: 33505021), lysosomal pH was observed to be higher in
TMEM175 KO cells during starvation, while differences were minimal under fed
conditions.
In the more recent studies (Parkinson's disease-risk protein TMEM175 is a
proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Meiqin Hu et al. Cell. 2022 PMID:
35750034 and pH regulates potassium conductance and drives a constitutive proton
current in human TMEM175. Wang Zheng et al. Sci Adv. 2022 PMID: 35333573),
it appears that the experiments were conducted without subjecting cells to starvation.
The lysosomal pH was measured in fed cells with/without Baf-A1. A possible
explanation, therefore, is that the effects of TMEM175 knockout on lysosomal pH
depends on the state of the cells. The phenotypes observed under fed conditions are
consistent across studies, and the phenotypes observed under starvation are not
contradictory.
In our experiment, measurements were taken using a plate reader, which
maintained an optimal temperature of 37°C for the cells. However, this instrument does
not provide a sterile environment, and extended measurement periods could introduce
additional variables. A two-hour timeframe was insufficient to observe the full effects
of the treatment, as BMDMs and culture media were typically harvested 4–10 hours
after cell debris treatment in our ELISA and Co-IP experiments. Therefore, we aimed
to accelerate the inflammasome activation. According to the present articles,
starvation
exacerbates lysosomal acidification defects and impairs lysosomal enzyme function (A
growth-factor-activated lysosomal K+ channel regulates Parkinson's pathology.
Jinhong Wie et al. Nature. 2021 PMID: 33505021). This inspired us to investigate
whether FBS starvation could promote the inflammasome activation. In preliminary
experiments, we observed that reducing FBS concentrations enhanced the
inflammasome activation. Specifically, at 1% FBS, IL-1β secretion was more robust.
Thus for our dynamic measurements of lysosomal pH, lysosomal calcium, cytosolic
calcium, and ROS, cells were treated in medium containing 1% FBS to observe changes
within a 2-hour window. These conditions resemble the “starved” state, and our results
were consistent with previous studies. We apologize for not clearly stating these details
in the original manuscript. To avoid further confusion, we repeated the experiments
under 10% FBS conditions and measured the lysosomal pH, lysosomal calcium,
cytosolic calcium, and ROS at the end of the treatment. Under these revised conditions,
we found that lysosomal pH in untreated Tmem175-/- BMDMs was slightly lower than
in WT BMDMs, whereas lysosomal pH in cell debris-treated Tmem175-/- BMDMs was
higher than in WT BMDMs. We propose that cell debris treatment creates a stress
condition that stimulates lysosomal activation, thereby revealing impaired lysosomal
acidification in Tmem175-deficient cells. These results parallels the response seen
under starvation. We also added the related information in our discussion section.
Additionally, we thank the reviewer for pointing out that M-CSF promotes
lysosomal acidification. Both Tmem175-/- and WT BMDMs were treated in medium
containing M-CSF, thus this factor is unlikely to influence the comparative conclusions
of our experiments.
In our pre-experiment, we found that decreasing FBS promoted the inflammasome
activation. Thus the dynamic changes of lysosomal pH, lysosomal calcium, cytosolic
calcium, and ROS were measured in medium containing 1% FBS to observe changes
within a 2-hour window
Fig.8 Calcium ions were involved in the promoted inflammasome activation in
TMEM175 knockout BMDMs. (a) Lysosomal pH were determined using
LysoSensor™ Yellow/Blue DND-160. The impeded lysosomal acidification in
Tmem175-/- BMDMs was observed after B16-F10 cell debris treatment.
2. It is also important to note that Ca²⁺ defects were proposed to cause ROS
elevation, which in turn promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-
18 secretion. Yet, lysosomal Ca²⁺ levels were shown to be normal in TMEM175
knockout (KO) cells (Figure 8b). These findings suggest that the
Ca²⁺/ROS/inflammasome effects may be secondary to lysosomal dysfunction
associated with TMEM175 deficiency.
Response: Thank you for your comment. It is indeed true that Ca²⁺ defects can reduce
ROS levels through mitochondrial-related mechanisms (Calcium and ROS: A mutual
interplay. Agnes Görlach et al. Redox Biol. 2015 PMID: 26296072). However, as
noted by Agnes Görlach et al., the relationship between Ca²⁺ and ROS is condition-
dependent. When the respiratory chain is inhibited or the Ca²⁺ overload occurs, a
positive correlation between Ca²⁺ and ROS can be observed. Additionally, we found a
study that demonstrated Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial damage, which led to ROS
generation and NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Critical role for calcium
mobilization in activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Tomohiko Murakami et al.
Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2012 PMID: 22733741). Therefore, the interplay between
Ca²⁺ and ROS may vary depending on the specific cellular conditions.
In contrast to previous studies suggesting that Ca²⁺ activates the NLRP3
inflammasome indirectly through ROS or other mechanisms (Critical role for calcium
mobilization in activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Tomohiko Murakami et al.
Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2012 PMID: 22733741 and The calcium-sensing receptor
regulates the NLRP3 inflammasome through Ca2+ and cAMP. Geun-Shik Lee et al.
Nature. 2012 PMID: 23143333), the primary hypothesis of our study is that Ca²⁺
directly participates in the ASC/NLRP3 interaction. We agree with your comment that
ROS may play a secondary role in this process. Although ROS could potentially be
involved in our mechanism, its contribution may be less significant than that of Ca²⁺.
This is supported by our findings showing that in vivo administration of NAC (a ROS
inhibitor) partially suppressed T cell immunity, whereas BAPTA-AM (a Ca²⁺ chelator)
completely suppressed T cell immunity.
Thank you again for sharing your insights on Ca²⁺ and ROS. This is an intriguing
area of research that could be explored more deeply in future studies. However in our
current work it seems that Ca²⁺ regulated NLRP3 activation directly, because EDTA-
Na2 treatment in cell lysate inhibited the ASC polymerization.
Figure S12. B16-F10 cell debris activated NLRP3 inflammasomes more
extensively in TMEM175 knockout BMDMs through lysosomal dysfunction. (k to
n) Recruitment and activation of CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were partially
inhibited by NAC in Tmem175-/- mice, however the IFN-γ and granzyme B expression
in CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were not significantly altered in Tmem175-/-
mice. (o to r) Recruitment, activation, IFN-γ expression, and granzyme B expression
in CD8+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were significantly diminished by NAC in
Tmem175-/- mice.
Fig.8 Calcium ions were involved in the promoted inflammasome activation in
TMEM175 knockout BMDMs. (k and l) CA-074 and BAPTA-AM suppressed the
recruitment and activation of CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) in Tmem175-/- mice.
BAPTA-AM suppressed the recruitment of CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) in
WT mice. (m and n) BAPTA-AM was more efficient than CA-074 in inhibiting IFN-γ
and granzyme B expression in CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) in Tmem175-/-
mice. (o to r) CA-074 and BAPTA-AM suppressed the recruitment, activation, IFN-γ
expression, and granzyme B expression of CD8+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) in
Tmem175-/- mice.
Fig.8 Calcium ions were involved in the promoted inflammasome activation in
TMEM175 knockout BMDMs. (d) Calcium chelation through BAPTA-AM inhibited
the IL-1β secretion (n = 3). Cells were treated by B16-F10 cell debris for 8 hours. (e)
Calcium chelation through BAPTA-AM or EDTA-Na2 blocked the interaction between
ASC and NLRP3 (n = 3). Cells were treated by B16-F10 cell debris for 4 hours.
Fig.10 Mechanisms of the elevated anti-tumor immunity in TMEM175 knockout
mice.
Tumor cell debris engulfed by BMDMs caused lysosomal membrane permeabilization
and cathepsin B leakage, which activated NLRP3 inflammasome. TMEM175 knockout
promoted lysosomal calcium efflux into cytoplasm thus promoting NLRP3
inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 secretion. IL-1β and IL-18 facilitated the
recruitment and activation of T cells and NKs. The augmented antigen cross-
presentation in Tmem175-/- BMDMs enhanced CD8+ T cell expansion and activation,
which was further promoted by IL-1β and IL-18.
3. Additionally, TMEM175 overexpression was reported to cause lysosomal hypo-
acidification (e.g., PMID: 35750034, 35333573). This raises the question: would
TMEM175 overexpression also exert effects in anti-tumor immunity?
Response: Thank you for your insightful inspiration about the TMEM175 and anti-
tumor immunity. In the previous works the role of TMEM175 over-expression was
analyzed in fed condition rather than during starvation or cell debris treatment. Notably,
TMEM175 over-expression resulted in its localization to the plasma membranes, in
addition to lysosomal membranes (Parkinson's disease-risk protein TMEM175 is a
proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Meiqin Hu et al. Cell. 2022 PMID:
35750034 and pH regulates potassium conductance and drives a constitutive proton
current in human TMEM175. Wang Zheng et al. Sci Adv. 2022 PMID: 35333573).
Thus it is difficult to determine whether TMEM175 over-expression could promote the
anti-tumor immunity under these conditions. However, we believe the key factor for
promoting the anti-tumor immunity is lysosomal dysfunction, which occurs during
starvation or cell debris treatment in TMEM175 knockout cells. Meiqin Hu et al.
reported that TMEM175 deficiency caused lysosomal over-acidification, impaired
proteolytic activity, and facilitated a-synuclein aggregation. Both their findings and
ours demonstrated that TMEM175 knockout induces lysosomal dysfunction, which is
critical for the downstream immune responses. TMEM175 overexpression is unlikely
to exert effects in anti-tumor immunity, because it is unlikely to cause lysosomal
dysfunction during cell debris treatment. Additionally, our results found that TMEM175
expression was higher in melanoma tissues than that in paracancerous tissues.
Furthermore, higher TMEM175 expression in TAMs is associated with
immunosuppressive CD206+ TAMs.
Fig.1 TMEM175 was elevated in melanoma tissues and related with M2-like TAMs
indicating that TMEM175 in myeloid cells should be deleted.
(a) Tissue chip of paired melanoma and paracancerous tissues was stained by anti-
TMEM175 to detect the expression of TMEM175 through IHC (n = 6 pairs).
TMEM175 was expressed more robustly in melanoma tissues than paracancerous
tissues. Scale bars indicate 500 μm for left panel and 50 μm for right panel.
TMEM175 positive area was calculated.
(b and c) Wild type mice were subcutaneously injected with 1×106 B16-F10 tumor
cells (n = 18 mice). Mice were humanely sacrificed at day 18 to analyze the TME
through FCM.
4. Some of the specific comments were not satisfactorily addressed. For instance,
in the response to major concern 1, this reviewer was unable to find the mentioned
40-55 kD band in the attached Figure 1.
Response: Thank you for your comment. The 40-55 kD band was too weak. In order to
show it clearly, we lengthened the exposure time of our WB membrane.
Fig.1 TMEM175 was elevated in melanoma tissues and related with M2-like TAMs
indicating that TMEM175 in myeloid cells should be deleted. (d) TMEM175
expression was obviously decreased in Tmem175-/- BMDMs. Lysates of Tmem175-/-
and WT BMDMs were analyzed by western blot using anti-TMEM175 antibody (n =
3).
5. Regarding the response to major concern 6, membrane leak can be easily
investigated using Na⁺ or NMDG⁺ containing recording solutions, as neither of
these ions is permeable to TMEM175 (PMID 26317472).
Response: Thank you for your comment. According to previously reported (TMEM175
Is an Organelle K(+) Channel Regulating Lysosomal Function. Chunlei Cang et al.
Cell. 2015, PMID: 26317472), we included the results obtained with the NMDG bath
solution. Our findings are consistent with those presented in Figure 7B-E of Chunlei
Cang's study, where NMDG in the bath solution inhibited the positive currents.
Fig.1 TMEM175 was elevated in melanoma tissues and related with M2-like TAMs
indicating that TMEM175 in myeloid cells should be deleted. (f) Lysosomal
potassium conductance in Tmem175-/- BMDMs was significantly decreased.
Lysosomes from Tmem175-/- and WT BMDMs were analyzed by lysosomal voltage
clamp. The current was recorded when the bath solution contained 150 mM K+ or 150
mM NMDG. Representative result of voltage clamp was displayed, and the average
current intensities in +100 mV and 150 mM K+ were compared (n = 5).
6. Overall, while the revised manuscript addresses some of the reviewers' concerns,
several critical issues regarding the mechanisms linking TMEM175 to Ca²⁺ dys-
homeostasis, oxidative stress, and lysosomal pH remain unresolved and require
further clarification.
Response: Thank you for your comment. Our previously presented data demonstrated
that ROS acted as a NLRP3 activator, although its role may be secondary to that of
calcium ions. We further investigated the Ca²⁺ dys-homeostasis through BafA1. BafA1
treatment decreased the lysosomal calcium concentration and increased the cytosolic
calcium, indicating the enhanced calcium efflux from lysosomes, which was in
accordance with previous report (Chloroquine modulates antitumor immune response
by resetting tumor-associated macrophages toward M1 phenotype. Degao Chen et al.
Nat Commun. 2018, PMID: 29491374). In conclusion, we appreciate your
constructive suggestions, which have significantly contributed to improving our
manuscript.
Fig.8 Calcium ions were involved in the promoted inflammasome activation in
TMEM175 knockout BMDMs. (b) Lysosomal calcium were determined using rhod-
dextran and AF488-dextran. The lower level of lysosomal calcium in Tmem175-/-
BMDMs than WT BMDMs was observed after B16-F10 cell debris treatment.
Neutralizing lysosomal pH with Bafilomycin A1 further decreased the lysosomal
calcium. (c) Cytoplasmic calcium were determined using Fluo-4-AM. The higher level
of cytoplasmic calcium in Tmem175-/- BMDMs than WT BMDMs was observed by
B16-F10 cell debris treatment. CA-074 did not obviously alter the cytoplasmic calcium
levels. Neutralizing lysosomal pH with Bafilomycin A1 further increased the
cytoplasmic calcium.
Reviewer #2
The authors have done an excellent job revising the manuscript, and my previous
comments have been adequately addressed.
Response: Thank you for your comment.
Reviewer #3
1. Authors did a great job to evaluate the effect of CA-074 and BAPTA-AM on the
inhibition of anti-tumor immunity in Tmem175-/- mice. However, without an in
vivo experiment using NAC, the contribution of ROS to the anti-tumor immunity
is still unclear.
Response: Thank you for your comment. We added the in vivo experiment using NAC
according to previously reported (Antioxidants accelerate lung cancer progression in
mice. Volkan I Sayin et al. Sci Transl Med. 2014, PMID: 24477002 and BACH1
Stabilization by Antioxidants Stimulates Lung Cancer Metastasis. Clotilde Wiel et al.
Cell. 2019, PMID: 31257027). And the related description were added in our
manuscript.
Figure S12. B16-F10 cell debris activated NLRP3 inflammasomes more
extensively in TMEM175 knockout BMDMs through lysosomal dysfunction. (g to
r) In order to investigate the influence of ROS on the anti-tumor immunity, Tmem175-
/- and WT mice (n = 5 mice) were subcutaneous implantation with 1×106 B16-F10
and treated with 1g/L NAC through drinking water after day 7. Mice were humanely
sacrificed on day 14 to weigh the tumors and analyze the TME through FCM. (h) The
anti-tumor effects of TMEM175 knockout was suppressed by NAC. (i) Expression of
MHC-II in TAMs (gated from CD45+ CD11b+ F4/80+ cells) was significantly
attenuated by NAC in Tmem175-/- mice. (j) Expression of CD206 in TAMs (gated from
CD45+ CD11b+ F4/80+ cells) was elevated by NAC in Tmem175-/- mice. (k to n)
Recruitment and activation of CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were partially
inhibited by NAC in Tmem175-/- mice, however the IFN-γ and granzyme B expression
in CD4+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were not significantly altered in Tmem175-/-
mice. (o to r) Recruitment, activation, IFN-γ expression, and granzyme B expression
in CD8+ T cells (gated from CD3+ cells) were significantly diminished by NAC in
Tmem175-/- mice.
2. Authors did a great amount of work on the mechanism by which cross-
presentation signals in TMEM175 KO macrophages was enhanced by IL-1β and
IL-18. However, the explanation is still unclear and too complicated. If authors
thought NF-kappaB pathway is the main mediator of IL-1β/IL18-enhanced cross-
presentation signal in macrophages, a treatment of Myd88 siRNA or related
inhibitors will help determine their hypothesis. Similarly, the roles of DEGs they
found could also be verified in macrophages with siRNA.
Response: Thank you for your comment. We used siRNA to inhibit Myd88 (a well-
established downstream signaling molecule of IL-1R) and Csf2rb (a shared DEG
regulated by IL-1β in both Tmem175-/- and WT group). Silencing Myd88 abrogated the
effects of IL-1β and IL-18. For IL-1β , better inhibitory effects were observed in
siMyd88, indicating that Myd88 is the main down-stream event. We did not silence
Csf2rb in IL-18 group, because it was not identified as a DEG in response to IL-18.
Thank you again for your constructive suggestions, which have greatly improved the
quality of our manuscript.
Figure S9. related to Figure 6. TMEM175 knockout augmented the cross-
presentation of tumor antigens. (e and f) In order to validate the down-stream events
of IL-1β and IL-18, we used siRNA to inhibit Myd88 (a known down-stream protein
of IL-1R) and Csf2rb (a common DEG up-regulated by IL-1β ). (e) Spleenic
lymphocytes from B16-F10-OVA tumor bearing mice were co-cultured with BMDMs
transfected with desired siRNA. (f) Silencing MyD88 inhibited the promoted CD8+ T
cell proliferation by IL-1β and IL-18. Silencing CSF2RB partially inhibited the

These results are opposite to what the authors showed in the previous submission, i.e., lysosomal hypo-acidification in the KO cells. Why were several figure panels regarding lysosomal acidification deleted in the current version? As mentioned repeatedly in the reviewers’ comments and now also in the Discussion of the manuscript, the effect of TMEM175 KO on lysosomal pH is controversial. After the two original studies in 2022 (PMID: 35750034, Cell 2022, and PMID: 35333573, Science Advances 2022) showed that TMEM175 is a lysosomal H+ channel and that TMEM175 KO cells exhibit lysosomal hyper-acidification, several follow-up studies have confirmed the hyper-acidification phenotype in TMEM175 KO cells, e.g., PMID: 37390818, Mol. peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear editor,
Thank you for your letter and the reviewers comments concerning our manuscript
Deficiency of lysosomal TMEM175 in myeloid macrophages exerts anti-tumor
immunity via inflammasome and cross-presentation pathway (NCOMMS-24-59454C)
submitted to Nature communications. Newly revised portions are highlighted in
yellow. The point-by-point response for the reviewers’ comments are listed as follows.
Reviewer #1
1. In the re-revised manuscript, it appears that some data were deleted or replaced
without explanation. For example, the new data in Figure 8 show lysosomal hyper-
acidification (no LPS and cell debris treatment) in the KO cells. These results are
opposite to what the authors showed in the previous submission, i.e., lysosomal
hypo-acidification in the KO cells. Why were several figure panels regarding
lysosomal acidification deleted in the current version?
Response: Thank you for your question. We apologize for the insufficient explanation
provided in the revised manuscript. In our previous submission, lysosomal pH,
lysosomal calcium, and cytosolic calcium levels were measured using a fluorescent
plate reader to monitor dynamic changes over a 2-hour period (i.e., dynamic
measurement). However, we found that a more accurate approach would be to collect
data at the end of the LPS and cell debris treatments (i.e., end-point measurement) for
two key reasons.
First, according to the instruction manual of the lysosomal pH probe LysoSensor™
Yellow/Blue DND-160 (Thermo), it is recommended to acquire the data within 5 min.
Therefore, we chose to measure the lysosomal pH once, immediately following the
desired treatment, rather than monitoring dynamic changes over a 2-hour period.
Second, although the plate reader maintained an optimal temperature of 37°C for
the cells, it does not provide a sterile environment with 5% CO . Moreover, the 2-hour
2
time frame was insufficient to capture the full effects of the LPS and cell debris
treatment, as BMDMs and culture media were harvested 4–10 hours after treatment in
our ELISA and Co-IP experiments. An extended dynamic measurement period would
not be accurate, as fluorescence readings were conducted outside a sterile environment
with 5% CO . Therefore, in the current version of the manuscript, we cultured the cells
2
under standard conditions (sterile, 37°C, and 5% CO ) and collected data on lysosomal
2
pH, lysosomal calcium, and cytosolic calcium once, immediately after treatment.
The discrepancy between the dynamic measurement (in our previous version) and
the end-point measurement (in the present version) arises from differences in the cell
treatment protocols. In the end-point measurement, BMDMs were cultured in complete
medium and treated with LPS and cell debris. In contrast, during the dynamic
measurement, BMDMs were cultured in medium containing 1% FBS in an attempt to
accelerate inflammasome activation by reducing FBS, as extended measurement
periods in the plate reader could introduce additional variables. In our preliminary
experiments, reducing FBS concentrations was found to expedite inflammasome
activation. However, these conditions mimicked a "starvation" state and did not
accurately reflect the effect of TMEM175 knockout on lysosomal pH under normal
culture conditions. Consequently, we preferred to replace the dynamic measurement
with the end-point measurement in our current manuscript.
In our pre-experiment, we found that decreasing FBS promoted the inflammasome
activation. Thus the dynamic changes of lysosomal pH, lysosomal calcium, and
cytosolic calcium were measured in medium containing 1% FBS to observe changes
within a 2-hour window in our previous manuscript.
2. As mentioned repeatedly in the reviewers’ comments and now also in the
Discussion of the manuscript, the effect of TMEM175 KO on lysosomal pH is
controversial. After the two original studies in 2022 (PMID: 35750034, Cell 2022,
and PMID: 35333573, Science Advances 2022) showed that TMEM175 is a
lysosomal H+ channel and that TMEM175 KO cells exhibit lysosomal hyper-
acidification, several follow-up studies have confirmed the hyper-acidification
phenotype in TMEM175 KO cells, e.g., PMID: 37390818, Mol. Cell 2023; PMID:
40865534, Neuron 2025; PMID: 40473625, Nature Communications 2025.
Response: Thank you for providing additional articles on the influence of TMEM175
knockout (KO) on lysosomal pH. We have carefully reviewed these references. It
appears that in these studies (PMID: 35750034, Cell 2022; PMID: 35333573, Science
Advances 2022; PMID: 37390818, Mol. Cell 2023; PMID: 40865534, Neuron 2025;
PMID: 40473625, Nature Communications 2025), WT and TMEM175 KO cells were
cultured in complete medium and subsequently stained with lysosomal pH probes. In
contrast, in our previous dynamic measurement, cells were measured in a "starvation"
state, as explained earlier, which resembles conditions in earlier studies (PMID:
26317472, Cell 2015; PMID: 28193887, PNAS 2017; PMID: 33505021, Nature 2021).
In our end-point measurement, cells were cultured in complete medium, yielding results
consistent with the articles you provided. Thus, the "contradictory" results between
different studies may stem from differences in cell treatment. Under resting conditions,
TMEM175 KO results in a hyper-acidification phenotype. However, when cells are
challenged with starvation or cell debris, TMEM175 KO induces an unstable lysosomal
pH and hypo-acidification.
3. Note that it is possible that LPS and cell debris treatment might affect lysosomal
acidification differently in WT versus KO cells. However, that was not what the
data from the earlier versions of the manuscript showed. Also, in the new Figure
8a, LPS induces lysosomal hyper-acidification in WT cells, yet the opposite results
were shown previously. Note that the proposed Ca2+ link can make sense only
when KO cells have a lysosomal hypo-acidification phenotype.
Response: Thank you for your comments. We acknowledge that TMEM175 knockout
may influence lysosomal acidification differently depending on whether cells are
cultured in complete medium or challenged with starvation or cell debris. In the present
Fig. 8a, LPS induced lysosomal hypo-acidification in WT cells, which aligns with our
previous data. As explained earlier, we believe that our current end-point measurement
provides a more accurate method for determining lysosomal pH, lysosomal calcium,
and cytosolic calcium, and thus we have replaced the figures accordingly. We suspect
that the "Ca²⁺ link" may not be the optimal model for describing cells treated with LPS
alone, as LPS treatment did not result in lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Fig.
7g). We hypothesize that lysosomal hypo-acidification, which occurs during lysosomal
membrane permeabilization induced by cell debris, promotes lysosomal calcium efflux,
thereby contributing to NLRP3 activation. As previously suggested, inhibiting
acidification by BafA1 in WT BMDMs mimicked the phenotypes of TMEM175 KO
BMDMs, which supported the "Ca²⁺ link" during the lysosomal membrane
permeabilization.
Fig. 8a Lysosomal pH were determined using LysoSensor™ Yellow/Blue DND-160.
The impeded lysosomal acidification in Tmem175-/- BMDMs was observed after B16-
F10 cell debris treatment.
Fig. 7g Tmem175-/- and WT BMDMs treated with LPS and B16-F10 cell debris were
fixed and permeabilized. Then cells were stained by cathepsin B rabbit mAb, cathepsin
D rabbit mAb, or cathepsin L rabbit mAb (n = 3). The spots of cathepsin B, cathepsin
D, and cathepsin L diffused in cytoplasm by cell debris treatment. Scale bars indicate
10 μm.
4. In addition, it appears that the Western blots in Figure 1d were also replaced,
yet it was mentioned in the rebuttal letter that the 40-55 kD band could only be
seen by increasing exposure time.
Response: Thank you for your comments. We have replaced this figure in response to
your previous suggestion to show the weak 40-55 kD bands. To address this, we
repeated the western blot assay and increased the exposure time to enhance detection.
5. In Figure 1f, I thought new experiments were performed with a K+ versus
NMDG+ comparison. However, although the data from WT cells are new, the data
from the KO cells and the statistical analysis are the same as before.
Response: Thank you for your comments. We have updated all of our voltage clamp
data and included the K⁺ versus NMDG comparison as requested.
Fig.1f Lysosomal potassium conductance in Tmem175-/- BMDMs was significantly
decreased. Lysosomes from Tmem175-/- and WT BMDMs were analyzed by lysosomal
voltage clamp. The current was recorded when the bath solution contained 150 mM K+
or 150 mM NMDG. Representative result of voltage clamp was displayed, and the
average current intensities in +100 mV with 150 mM K+ or 150 mM NMDG were
compared (n = 5).
Reviewer #3 & #4
1. The new in vivo experiment with NAC confirmed the contribution of ROS to
the anti-tumor immunity in Tmem175-/- mice. However, it seems that NAC
administration caused no phenotypes in control mice. Considering authors showed
NAC was able to suppress inflammasome activation and IL-1β secretion in control
macrophages (Supplemental Fig. 12C,D), they should give an explanation in the
manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your comments. NAC partially inhibited the anti-tumor
immunity in Tmem175-/- mice, suggesting that the elevated ROS levels in Tmem175-/-
macrophages contributed to the anti-tumor immunity. This inhibitory effects were not
as pronounced in WT mice, which could be owed to the lower ROS activation in WT
mice. Although NAC inhibited the inflammasome activation in WT BMDMs in vitro,
its inhibitory effects on the immune microenvironment in vivo were more evident in
mice with higher basal ROS activation. When the ROS in macrophages was low,
inhibiting ROS did not further suppress downstream events. The related explanation
has been added in our manuscript (RESULTS section line 548-552).
2. The reduction the promoted CD8+ T cell proliferation by siRNA treatment
seems convincing. A measurement of knock down efficiency in macrophages by
siRNA would further elevate the solidity of this data.
Response: Thank you for your comments. We confirmed the knockdown efficiency by
FCM, and the data have been added in Supplementary Fig. 9g and h.
Figure S9. (g and h) The decreased MyD88 and CSF2RB expression by siRNA was
confirmed by FCM.
All the point-by-point responses are presented above. We are willing to make further
revision to improve the manuscript. We look forward to your decision.
Yours sincerely,
Xiawei Wei, Ph. D
Full Professor and Director of Lab of Cancer Drug Target and Aging Research
State Key Laboratory of Biotherapy,
West China Hospital, Sichuan University

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Discovering more targets is of great importance for developing alternative interventions for tumor therapy. The roles of transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175) in neurodegeneration diseases have been reported, however its functions in tumor immune surveillance are not known. We show that TMEM175 conditional knockout in macrophages inhibits the tumor growth and metastasis through promoting the anti-tumor immunity in the tumor microenvironment (TME), including elevated M1-like polarization, reduced M2-like polarization, and facilitated recruitment and activation of T cells and nature killer cells (NKs). The anti-tumor immunity is abrogated by caspase-1 inhibitor VX-765, anti-IL-1β, and anti-IL-18. Tmem175−/− bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) show enhanced tumor antigen cross-presentation that is further strengthened by IL-1β and IL-18. NLRP3 is robustly elicited in Tmem175−/− BMDMs by the tumor cell debris through lysosomal permeabilization and cathepsin B leakage. Finally, Tmem175−/− mice are more responsive to anti-PD-1. Our works imply TMEM175 to be a potential target for immunotherapy.

---

## Introduction

Immune surveillance in TME is crucial for the clearance of tumor cells. Diving into the mechanisms of immune surveillance could help us find more targets to propagate the anti-tumor immunity. Immunotherapy of malignant tumors have developed a constellation of therapeutic methods providing diverse choice for clinicians1. For example, anti-PD-1 antibody is commonly applied in melanoma therapy, however, drug resistance has been reported repeatedly2. Developing novel immunotherapy strategies may help improving anti-tumor immunity through alternative mechanisms.

Macrophages are a subset of crucial immune cells in TME, whose M2-like polarization and other behaviors have been shown to promote the tumor progression3,4. M2-like tumor associated macrophages (TAMs) attenuate the anti-tumor immunity through diverse mechanisms, including secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines5, up-regulation of immune-suppressive PD-L16, and down-regulation of immune-stimulatory major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II)7, resulting in the immune evasion. On the contrary, reprogramming M2-like TAMs into M1-like TAMs through some interventions, such as TLR ligands8, chloroquine9, and hydroxychloroquine10, restored the recruitment and activation of T cells. Notably, the behaviors of TAMs are much more complicated beyond polarization. For instance, TAMs have been demonstrated to degrade extracellular matrix and promote the tumor invasion via secreted cathepsins and cathepsins in lysosomes4,11,12.

Lysosomes are the organelles that profoundly mediate the behaviors of macrophages in many diseases13. Macrophages intake extracellular substances through phagocytosis and transport them into lysosomes, where the low pH provides an optimal condition for nearly 60 kinds of hydrolytic enzymes13,14. The acidic luminal pH in lysosomes is maintained by the vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase) and other ion channels on lysosomal membrane. The v-ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to pump protons into lysosomes, and at the same time, cation efflux or anion influx through other ion channels is needed to balance the transmembrane potential15,16. TMEM175 is a potassium channel on lysosomal membrane, whose knockout causes incapacity to maintain acidic luminal pH during starvation17,18. Additionally, later research also illustrates the H+ permeability of TMEM17519,20. Present results have revealed that the dysfunction of TMEM175 causes Parkinson disease18,21. However researches focusing on the potential role of TMEM175 in the tumor immunity is limited. The crosstalk between lysosomal proton and calcium mediates the polarization of macrophages and anti-tumor immunity9. We thus hypothesize that TMEM175 might influence the homeostasis of lysosomal ions and regulate the behaviors of TAMs.

Dysfunction of lysosomes can activate inflammasome signal and alter the anti-tumor immunity in TME22. Inflammasome signals are composed of several kinds of intracellular sensors including, NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3), NLR family pyrin domain containing 1 (NLRP1), NLR family apoptosis inhibitory protein (NAIP)/NLR family CARD domain containing 4 (NLRC4), absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), and Pyrin that recognize various danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)23. NLRP3 is the most extensively studied inflammasome sensor, partially because it can be activated by diverse stimuli, while the others can only be provoked by specific kinds of substances. Activation of NLRP3 requires signal 1 that initiates the expression of proteins in NLRP3 pathway by ligands of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and signal 2 that engages assembly of NLRP3 inflammasomes by DAMPs and PAMPs resulting in the secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18)24. Rupture of lysosomes and leakage of lysosomal content have been shown to elicit NLRP3 signal during the pathology of atherosclerosis25. In TME, NLRP3 activation has been observed in not only tumor cells but also stromal cells26–29. Both pro- and anti-tumor effects of NLRP3 activation have been reported in massive researches26,27,30–32. Although many details about the relationship between NLRP3 inflammasomes and tumor progression remain fuzzy, some inhibitors of NLRP3 pathways have been developed and tested for their anti-tumor potential33–35. Interestingly, an NLRP3 activator, BMS-986299, was also tested in a clinical research for solid cancers (NCT03444753). More investigations about the role of NLRP3 in TME are needed for a better understanding of inflammasomes in tumors.

Here, we found that conditional knockout of TMEM175 in macrophages significantly attenuated the tumor growth of melanoma B16-F10 and lung cancer LL-2 subcutaneous tumors, as well as the lung metastasis of B16-F10. TMEM175 knockout increased the MHC-II+ M1-like macrophages and decreased the CD206+ M2-like macrophages, resulting in the fostered recruitment and activation of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and NKs in TME. The effects of TMEM175 knockout were underpinned by the inflammasome activation, since VX-765, anti-IL-1β, anti-IL-18, and Nlrp3 silencing abrogated the anti-tumor effects. Due to the tempered lysosomal degradation, Tmem175−/− BMDMs demonstrated accentuated tumor antigen cross-presentation that was further strengthened by IL-1β and IL-18. We also found how Tmem175−/− BMDMs possessed robust inflammasome activation. The cell debris engulfed by BMDMs caused the lysosomal membrane permeabilization, resulting in the NLRP3 activation by the released cathepsin B (CTSB). During this process, the potentiated cytosolic calcium ions that might be owed to the attenuated lysosomal acidification could be the key factor facilitating the NLRP3 activation in Tmem175−/− BMDMs. Finally, the potential of clinical application of TMEM175 knockout was further verified by the result that Tmem175−/− mice showed better response to anti-PD-1 therapy.

In summary, conditional knockout of Tmem175 in macrophages demonstrates obvious anti-tumor immunity in mice. The underlying mechanisms are compromised by the cross-presentation and NLRP3 inflammasome, enhanced by the lysosomal dysfunction in Tmem175−/− BMDMs. Our findings reveal the role of TMEM175 in tumor immunity, highlighting its potential in immunotherapy. Development of interventions targeting TMEM175 is needed for alternative immunotherapy strategies in the future.
